newsitem.title: CANADA: Reuters poll shows Canada's Reform party gaining.
newsitem.headline: Reuters poll shows Canada's Reform party gaining.

text.p: Canada's right-wing Reform Party is gaining momentum as the federal election campaign races toward the June 2 vote, a Reuters poll released on Monday shows.
The daily tracking poll, conducted by Zogby International over the past three days, shows support for Reform growing to 19.3 percent from 16.9 percent in the Reuters-Zogby survey on Sunday.

Monday's results also showed the ruling Liberals maintaining their solid lead nationally, with 42.2 percent support, down slightly from Sunday's 43.8 percent and from 45.4 percent in the broad Zogby poll of May 16.
The Conservatives were second nationally at 20.6 percent, up from 20.2 percent on Sunday.
Reform posted the biggest gains in its Western Canada strongholds of British Columbia and in Alberta, where it advanced to 51 percent from 48 percent on Sunday.

"Aggressive and focused advertising on the part of Reform, where it is smartly targeting its base in the Western provinces, has shown a marked increase in support in that area," pollster John Zogby said.
The surge in support for Reform comes a few days after the party aired controversial campaign ads suggesting that Quebec-born politicians do not have what it takes to keep Quebec from leaving Canada.
The poll suggested party loyalty was soft and fluid leading into the June 2 election, Zogby said.
The percentage of undecided voters grew to 32.6 percent on Monday from 31.2 percent on Sunday, suggesting voters were changing their minds about their vote.

"Part of it is not surprising," said Zogby. "When you have four candidates beating up on one candidate, it suggests that support for the Liberals will go down. But as support for the Liberals declines, people may not have immediately made up their mind where the alternative is."

The poll also quizzed Canadians on whether they thought the country was heading in the right direction. As in Sunday's results, just under half of respondents on Monday felt Canada was headed in the right direction, while 32.1 percent thought the country was on the wrong track.
Among the disgruntled respondents, Reform attracted 35.2 percent, followed by the Conservatives at 20.5 percent, the Liberals 19.8 percent, the NDP 13.8 percent and the Bloc Quebecois 8.2 percent.

"Today's numbers suggest for the first time that one party may be positioning itself to capture the 'wrong direction voters,'" Zogby said in a telephone interview. "At this point it looks like Reform."

The surveys are the result of a three-day rolling average of 1,014 voters. The rolling averages began on Sunday, with Monday being the second day of the rolling poll. More results are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Monday's national results showed the left-wing New Democrats slipping to 9.9 percent from Sunday's 10.6 percent, while the separatist Bloc Quebecois, which is fielding candidates only in French-speaking Quebec, fell to 6.3 percent from 6.6 percent.
The poll showed a tight three-way race in Quebec among the Liberals, Conservatives and Bloc, but a firm Liberal grasp in Ontario and the Prairie provinces.
The poll has a margin of error for the national sample of 3.2 percentage points. For provincial breakdowns, the margin of error is higher.
